cards.headline: Big Brothers Big Sisters returns Big Taste of Martin County fundraiser to Stuart
cards.teaser: Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties will hold the Big Taste of Martin County food and spirits event October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart to support mentoring programs.
cards.body:
Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for October 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart. The annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. Guests can sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights.

 The event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big, according to Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties. The nonprofit said community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. More information about the event and mentorship opportunities is available through Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art to host recycled fishing line bracelet workshop Aug. 8
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program starting at 10 a.m. Aug. 8.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will host a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways.

 Participants also can learn about the Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program.

 Visitors can then participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum's summer exhibitions throughout the day. James Prosek: At Work is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day.

cards.headline: Stuart and Palm City events highlight weekend activities across Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: The Treasure Coast offers several family events this weekend, including a Christmas in July vendor market in Palm City and the weekly Rockn Riverwalk concert series in Stuart. The
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast offers several family events this weekend, including a Christmas in July vendor market in Palm City and the weekly Rockn Riverwalk concert series in Stuart. The Christmas in July event takes place Saturday at 10 a.m. at 2001 SW Murphy Road in Palm City. The market will feature food trucks, an ornament decorating station and vendors.

 The Downtown Business Association of Stuart is hosting Rockn Riverwalk on Sunday at 1 p.m. on St. Lucie Avenue in Stuart. The free open-air concert series takes place every Sunday on the Riverwalk Stage, offering live music on the waterfront.

 Several additional events are scheduled in Palm Beach County this weekend. The Boynton Beach Night Market returns Saturday at 5 p.m. at Centennial Park and Amphitheater. The free event features vendors, food and live music connecting residents to the local business community.

 A back-to-school family festival will take place Sunday from noon to 5 p.m. at 7715 Forest Hill Boulevard in West Palm Beach, featuring games, food, music and a school supply giveaway. A school supply drive will also be held Saturday and Sunday at 10 a.m. at a Walmart at 101 N. Congress Avenue in Lake Park, with donations distributed at a Back to School Bash in August.

cards.headline: Boca Raton TLC Program Offers Summer Service Projects for South Florida Families
cards.teaser: B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program connects volunteers with hands-on service projects ranging from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking and literacy efforts.
cards.body:
B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program is offering South Florida families a range of hands-on service projects this summer, from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking, literacy efforts and care for seniors. Led by Summer Faerman, the program connects volunteers of all ages with mitzvah opportunities, or meaningful good deeds, as part of the congregation's broader community outreach efforts.

 The TLC Program stands for Tzedakah, Learning and Chesed, and has made service a central part of synagogue life since 2012. The program provides a way for individuals and families to put Jewish values into action while helping people in need across South Florida. It addresses multiple community concerns including hunger, homelessness, literacy, elder care, vulnerable populations and special needs. Organizers emphasize that the projects are open to everyone in the community, not only members of B'nai Torah Congregation, with the goal of making service practical, welcoming and easy to begin.

 Participants can volunteer in various ways throughout the summer. Projects include making sandwiches, serving meals, collecting and cleaning shoes, stocking Little Free Pantries, preparing backpacks for back-to-school efforts, creating Bags of Hope and helping seniors with technology. Organizers plan to demonstrate volunteer projects such as wrapping presents, making flower arrangements, preparing sandwiches, collecting shoes and assembling supplies for people in need. The variety of options allows families to choose activities that match their interests and schedules.

 As summer continues, the TLC Program offers families a way to stay connected, teach children about giving back and support neighbors throughout South Florida. B'nai Torah Congregation says the program is built around the idea that small acts of service can strengthen the larger community. More information about the TLC Program is available through B'nai Torah Congregation's website.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Food Bank serves 2,500 hot meals daily to children at 35 summer sites
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Food Bank in Lake Worth Beach is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program while school is out.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Food Bank is serving approximately 2,500 hot meals each day to nearly 1,250 children through Florida's Summer BreakSpot program, according to Food Bank leaders. The nonprofit organization supports more than 35 Summer BreakSpot sites across Palm Beach County while school is out for the summer. During a live Shining A Light broadcast on WPTV, CEO Jamie Kendall and Culinary Director Chef Doug Barg gave viewers a behind-the-scenes look inside the Michelle Hagerty Community Kitchen, where meals are prepared and loaded onto trucks for early morning deliveries across the county.

 The organization prepared more than 36,000 hot meals in June alone. According to the Palm Beach County Food Bank, hunger doesn't take a summer break, highlighting the need for continued support during the summer months. The Summer BreakSpot program provides free meals to children and teens 18 and younger during the summer when school cafeterias are closed. Food Bank leaders said the meals are distributed through partner locations across Palm Beach County to help families facing food insecurity during the summer. Kendall said the Food Bank's partnership with Summer BreakSpot helps ensure children continue receiving nutritious meals while school is out.

 During the broadcast, viewers got a close look at the large-scale kitchen operation responsible for preparing meals daily. Chef Barg walked viewers through the food production process, showing how culinary teams prepare, package and organize meals before they are loaded onto delivery trucks. The loading dock operation featured drivers and volunteers preparing for morning deliveries to Summer BreakSpot sites throughout Palm Beach County. The Palm Beach County Food Bank said volunteers and community support are critical to maintaining the program during the busy summer season.

 The Palm Beach County Food Bank is located at 701 Boutwell Road, Suite A-1, in Lake Worth Beach. Food Bank leaders said the organization continues seeking volunteers, donations and community partnerships to support its mission of reducing childhood hunger in Palm Beach County. Families looking for Summer BreakSpot meal locations can find participating sites throughout the county during the summer months.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers sworn in as chairman of Florida Sheriffs Association
hero.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. F
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. Flowers now leads the statewide organization that brings together sheriffs from across Florida to develop strategies for leading their counties.

 The Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors includes sheriffs from throughout the state who work together on law enforcement strategies and leadership issues affecting county agencies. Flowers served as vice chairman of the board during the previous year before taking on the chairmanship role.

 The swearing-in ceremony took place Thursday, marking Flowers' elevation to the top position in the statewide law enforcement organization. The association serves as a platform for sheriffs to collaborate on policies and approaches to county law enforcement challenges.

 Flowers continues to serve as sheriff of Indian River County while taking on the additional responsibilities of chairing the Florida Sheriffs Association board. The organization coordinates efforts among the state's 67 elected sheriffs on issues ranging from training standards to legislative priorities.

cards.headline: Postal worker arrested for stealing winning Florida Lottery ticket from mail in Miami
cards.teaser: A United States Postal Service letter carrier was arrested July 23 on charges of stealing a winning Pick 4 lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize. Lekaysh
cards.body:
A United States Postal Service letter carrier was arrested July 23 on charges of stealing a winning Pick 4 lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize. Lekaysha Lockhart, who worked as a USPS letter carrier, faces charges including grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft.

 The arrest followed a joint investigation by the Florida Lottery Division of Security and the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General. A Florida Lottery player reported that a winning Pick 4 ticket she mailed never reached its intended destination. A Florida Lottery Inspector determined the ticket had been redeemed by Lockhart on June 19 at the Florida Lottery's Miami District Office.

 Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it. Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection. Dixon commended the Division of Security for their investigative work and thanked partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration.

 Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said. The Florida Lottery's Office of Communications released details of the arrest in a news release.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds holds commanding lead in Florida GOP governor's race with three weeks until primary
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds maintains a dominant position in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary with fewer than three weeks remaining before the Aug. 19 election, buoyed by Pre
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds maintains a dominant position in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary with fewer than three weeks remaining before the Aug. 19 election, buoyed by President Donald Trump's endorsement, superior name recognition and a significant financial advantage over his three main rivals. A political committee supporting Donalds this week released a statewide television and digital ad centered on affordability, showing Donalds playing basketball with his sons while promising to cut property taxes, lower insurance rates and reduce housing costs.

 A public Cygnal survey conducted July 12-13 found Donalds leading with 43 percent, followed by investor James Fishback at 12 percent, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins at 11 percent and former House Speaker Paul Renner at 2 percent.

 Another 31 percent remained undecided. The survey included 500 likely Republican primary voters and had a margin of error of 4.38 percentage points. Collins' campaign released an internal poll this week showing a closer contest, with Donalds at 46 percent and Collins at 30 percent, though public polling has generally shown Collins much farther behind.

 Fishback won a courtroom victory this week after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Collins' attempt to remove him from the ballot. Collins had pointed to Fishback's 2020 vote in Washington, D.C., his purchase of a condominium there and tax, mortgage and homestead records as evidence that Fishback had established residency outside Florida. Frank ruled that Collins failed to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

 Fishback responded by calling on Collins to resign as lieutenant governor, calling the legal challenge an attempt to rig the election. Collins dismissed the demand and said his team had not yet decided whether to appeal.

 Renner is using his closing campaign ads to emphasize his record as House speaker, including the expansion of school-choice programs and conservative legislation passed while he led the chamber. Vote-by-mail ballots have already been distributed for the Aug. 19 primary. Florida's mandatory early-voting period begins Aug. 8 and continues through Aug. 15, though counties may offer additional days. On the Democratic side, David Jolly is already focusing his attacks on Donalds, this week promising to halt new AI data-center construction until Florida develops stronger protections for its water supply, electric grid, communities and consumer privacy.

cards.headline: Florida judge considers challenge to Amendment 3 ballot language on property taxes
cards.teaser: A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or am
cards.body:
A Leon County circuit judge heard arguments Wednesday over whether the ballot title and summary for Amendment 3, a November property-tax measure, fairly explains the proposal or amounts to political advocacy. The amendment would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 for people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, reduce the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, and require local governments to spend remaining property-tax revenue on public needs such as public safety, schools, infrastructure and natural resources.

 Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank heard arguments in three consolidated lawsuits challenging the title and summary scheduled to appear on November ballots. The challengers include the nonprofit Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language, several former mayors, former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes and former Democratic U.S. Rep.

 Al Lawson Jr. They argue the amendment's title, 'Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes,' and phrases promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness are biased, inaccurate and designed to persuade voters. Plaintiffs' attorney Jamie Cole told the court the language crosses a line and called it the worst example of a biased ballot question he has seen.

 Frank did not immediately rule, instead ordering attorneys to submit proposed decisions by 5 p.m. Monday.

 Attorneys representing the attorney general, secretary of state and Department of State urged Frank to uphold the language. State attorney Ben Gibson argued the title and summary must be read together and that Florida law requires them to explain only the amendment's chief purpose, not every possible consequence or implementation detail. The challengers must prove the title and summary are clearly and conclusively defective, not merely that different wording could have been better, Gibson said.

 The Legislature approved the proposal during a June special session, passing it 75-26 in the House and 30-9 in the Senate. Because it is a proposed constitutional amendment, it was not subject to the governor's signature or veto. It needs support from at least 60% of voters in November.

 A July analysis by Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions of the amendment would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year. The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Election officials told the court that county supervisors may begin printing ballots Aug. 27, adding urgency to the case and any appeal. If Frank finds all of the ballot statements defective and appeals are declined or exhausted, Florida law gives Attorney General James Uthmeier 10 days to submit corrected wording.

cards.headline: Florida executes former police officer convicted of killing 11-year-old girl in 1987
cards.teaser: James Aren Duckett, 68, was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m. Tuesday at Florida State Prison, the first of two executions carried out by the state in a single day.
cards.body:
Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while he was working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987. He declined to make a final statement and showed no response several minutes into the execution when the prison warden shook him and shouted his name. Duckett became the 11th Florida inmate executed this year.

 The girl's relatives spoke of decades of suffering after the execution. Dorthy Tula, the victim's mother, said she waited nearly 40 years to have him dead before breaking down. Tracy Mcfall-Buskirk, the girl's cousin, said the man took advantage of his badge. The execution was part of the first double execution in Florida in more than six decades and the first time any state has carried out two executions in one day since Arkansas in 2017.

 Florida has now conducted 12 executions to date in 2026, more than all other states combined. Gov. Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty in the U.S. in 1976.

cards.headline: Judge keeps Fishback on Florida Republican primary ballot, rejects Collins residency challenge
cards.teaser: Lt. Gov. Jay Collins failed to remove gubernatorial candidate James Fishback from Florida's Republican primary ballot after a judge ruled Collins did not present enough evidence to prove Fishback abandoned his Florida residency.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins failed to present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and access to the ballot. Collins argued that Fishback failed to satisfy the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the general election. Collins attorneys pointed to records showing Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income-tax returns and signed mortgage documents identifying a condominium there as his principal residence.

 Fishback testified that he never intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. He described the Washington property as a second residence or investment and said he signed the mortgage documents without closely reviewing them. Frank acknowledged that Fishback's filings could potentially create legal or regulatory consequences in Washington.

 But he found that they did not establish that Fishback intended to surrender his Florida domicile. The judge also cited Fishback's Florida upbringing, family connections, drivers license, vehicle registration, voting history and business ties to the state.

 The order leaves Fishback on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot. Fishback turned his courtroom victory into a campaign counterattack Tuesday, demanding that Collins resign and accusing the lieutenant governor of abusing his office and the public trust by pursuing the residency challenge. Collins rejected the resignation demand and said the ruling would not change his campaign.

 A Cygnal survey conducted July 12 and 13 placed U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Trump-endorsed Republican frontrunner, at 43%, Fishback at 12%, Collins at 11% and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2%.

cards.headline: Over 150 assisted living residents remain displaced after Bradenton roof collapse
cards.teaser: More than 150 Florida residents remain scattered across assisted living facilities throughout the Tampa Bay area days after a partial roof collapse forced an emergency evacuation at Aviata at Bradenton Villas early Sunday morning.
cards.body:
Family members and advocates say loved ones have been placed in facilities as far south as Englewood and as far north as New Port Richey, with medical records, wheelchairs and personal belongings still trapped inside the damaged building. George Mendez, who holds power of attorney for 93-year-old Alfred Perani, came to the facility Monday after repeated phone calls to Aviata Health Group went unanswered.

 Perani, who has been a resident at Aviata at Bradenton Villas for three years, was evacuated to a facility in Palm Harbor. Mendez found an available bed at another facility in Bradenton to bring his friend closer to home but says he cannot complete the transfer without Perani's medical records.

 In a joint statement released Monday, the City of Bradenton and Manatee County provided new details about why the Fire Marshal ordered the emergency evacuation. Officials say the partial roof collapse compromised multiple building systems essential to safe operation, including fire protection, electrical and air conditioning systems. Damage to critical support areas necessary for resident care, combined with the inability to safely complete a full structural assessment during the emergency, made it unsafe for residents to remain.

 The emergency response involved the City of Bradenton Fire Department, Manatee County Public Safety and Emergency Medical Services, and multiple regional partners. All 157 residents were evacuated by approximately 4 a.m. Sunday.

 The City of Bradenton is in charge of the building assessment. A city spokesperson confirmed that city officials and the Fire Marshal were on-site at Aviata Monday, along with flooding and restoration specialists. According to the joint statement, the property owner's structural engineer is responsible for evaluating the building, and any determination regarding the cause of the collapse will be based on that evaluation. The Agency for Health Care Administration is conducting site visits at the facilities where residents were relocated as part of its state regulatory oversight.

hero.headline: Martin County School District cuts 3 bus routes, saving $255,000
hero.teaser: The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions.
hero.body:
The Martin County School District has approved a consolidation of bus routes that officials say will save $255,000 without affecting students or eliminating any driver positions. The school board voted Tuesday unanimously to reduce the number of bus routes by 3, bringing the total from 58 to 55 ahead of the upcoming school year. District officials say all bus stops will remain the same and students will not be impacted by the change.

Superintendent Michael Maine said the district has 55 routes and roughly 56 drivers, meaning all routes are covered. The $255,000 in savings reflects a reduced transportation budget and will not be redirected to a specific expense, according to the school district. Parents have mixed reactions. Marino Reyes and Tiffany Gugumuck expressed support for the financial decision. Ken Winstanley wondered where the money will go.

Michael Skinner, the President of the local AFSCME labor union chapter, voiced concerns during public comment on behalf of the bus drivers. He said feedback from bus drivers indicated their routes or buses are always full and cutting routes is not a good idea. Transportation Director Ruth Spires pushed back on that concern, noting that the buses hold a maximum of 77 passengers and are not operating at capacity.

Spires confirmed that no drivers were let go as part of the consolidation. The district was already challenged with a shortage last year, so the drivers were already covering the routes that were merged, Spires said. Drivers will be paid for any additional hours they work as a result of the consolidation. The district said it is confident it will maintain the same level of service with fewer buses on the road.

cards.headline: Stuart man jailed after fleeing traffic stop, leading police chase into Martin County
cards.teaser: David Allen Kingsley Jr., 31, was arrested July 28 after fleeing a Stuart Police officer during a traffic stop and leading law enforcement on a chase that ended in Martin County wi
cards.body:
David Allen Kingsley Jr., 31, was arrested July 28 after fleeing a Stuart Police officer during a traffic stop and leading law enforcement on a chase that ended in Martin County with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office and Florida Highway Patrol. Kingsley remains in the Martin County Jail on a $40,000 bond.

 A Stuart Police officer stopped Kingsley on an equipment violation the evening of July 28. After the officer discovered that Kingsley's driver's license was revoked, Kingsley took off. Kingsley led officers on a brief pursuit within the City of Stuart, striking another vehicle before continuing out of the city.

 Kingsley continued driving recklessly into Martin County jurisdiction, where deputies with the Martin County Sheriff's Office and troopers with the Florida Highway Patrol assisted in the pursuit. The vehicle was ultimately stopped, and Kingsley surrendered without further incident.

 Kingsley was charged with two counts of fleeing eluding law enforcement, one count of leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, failure to obey an officer's order to stop, reckless driving, and driving while license suspended or revoked. He was in the Martin County Jail as of July 30 on those charges.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man caught on surveillance video stealing thousands of dollars worth of tequila
cards.teaser: Michael Ruiz, 31, was caught on camera stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack at a Martin County liquor store and walking out with three cases without paying.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office has released surveillance video that investigators say shows a Port St. Lucie man stealing thousands of dollars worth of tequila from a local liquor store. According to deputies, 31-year-old Michael Ruiz was caught on camera stuffing bottles of tequila into a backpack while inside the store.

 The video also allegedly shows Ruiz entering a storage room, grabbing three cases of tequila and walking out without paying. Authorities say the stolen alcohol was worth thousands of dollars. Ruiz was later arrested in neighboring St. Lucie County on unrelated charges after police said he was driving under the influence.

 Investigators believe Ruiz may be connected to several other recent tequila thefts reported across the area and are continuing to look into those cases. The Martin County Sheriff's Office released the surveillance footage as part of its investigation and is asking anyone with information about similar incidents to contact law enforcement.

cards.teaser: Renters across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties say the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances, while a local real estate agent reports the rental market has leveled off.
cards.body:
Renters on the Treasure Coast say the cost of living is putting a strain on their finances. Jesse Espinoza, a renter in Martin County, said the price of rent is taking a toll on his ability to afford basic expenses including food and pet care. A resident identified as Mike said his rent has gone up significantly since he first moved to the area, now three times more expensive than when he arrived.

 Indian River County has the lowest average rents in the region, ranging from $1,650 to $2,200 a month. St. Lucie County averages between $2,100 to $2,300 a month.

 Decowski said more rental inventory is coming to the market, which could push prices down, though inflation remains a wildcard. cards.headline: Martin County commissioners face pushback on proposed changes to beach shark fishing rules
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners heard strong public opposition during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders .
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners heard strong public opposition during Tuesday morning's meeting as residents, local surfers, and marine experts urged local leaders to keep strict limits on beachside shark fishing. The debate centers on potential language changes to local ordinances regarding land-based shark fishing, a practice where anglers deploy lines from the shore using heavy gear, kayaks, or drones to drop bait and chum into deeper waters.

 During public comments, speakers warned that chumming, releasing fish parts and blood into the surf to attract sharks, endangers swimmers, surfers, and families. Local surfer Jay Noyes said he has been caught in shark fishing lines. Dottie Lanci, a member of the Hutchinson Island Preservation Initiative, strongly opposed any effort to loosen existing restrictions that ban shark baiting on lifeguard-protected beaches.

 Lanci called on commissioners to prioritize safety and extend the ban across all county beaches, citing an incident she witnessed outside her home where anglers used drones to drop chum in the water. She noted that other Florida municipalities, such as Miami Beach, passed local bans on land-based shark fishing earlier this year.

 Safety concerns over shark activity on local beaches carry weight with many residents. In August 2017, a 3-year-old girl named Violet Veatch was bitten on the leg by a suspected bull shark while wading in shallow water at Bathtub Reef Beach in Martin County. The toddler's mother, Jessica Veatch, later pushed for stricter local beach safety regulations, believing the shark was drawn to the crowded swimming area by spearfishermen carrying bloody fish through the water.

 Justin Grubich, a marine conservation expert and local surfer who moved to the area from Fort Lauderdale, urged the commission to maintain strong local restrictions. Pointing to recent research presented at statewide conservation forums, Grubich warned that regular baiting near popular beaches conditions wildlife. Commissioners did not take immediate action on the ordinance during the meeting, but requested further review of local public safety boundaries alongside state FWC regulations.

hero.headline: 86-year-old woman dies after Port St. Lucie intersection crash
hero.teaser: An 86-year-old woman died Thursday after she pulled into the path of an SUV at a Port St. Lucie intersection and was struck. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savo
hero.body:
An 86-year-old woman died after pulling into the path of an SUV at a Port St. Lucie intersection Thursday afternoon. The crash happened at about 2:30 p.m. at Southwest Savona Boulevard and Southwest Lawndale Avenue.

Marie R. Martin was driving a 2006 Hyundai Elantra west on Lawndale Avenue when she entered the intersection from near a stop sign and failed to yield to a northbound 2026 Honda HR-V, according to Port St. Lucie police investigators. The Honda, driven by a 17-year-old boy, struck the drivers side of Martin's car. Body camera video recorded after the crash shows the Hyundai off the roadway near a cluster of palm trees, with visible damage to its drivers side and emergency crews working around the vehicle. The Honda also came to rest on the grass nearby, close to vegetation and a roadside sign.

Martin had to be extricated from the Hyundai before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with critical injuries. She later died despite efforts to save her. The teenage driver of the Honda was not injured.

The Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit continues to investigate the crash. Port St. Lucie police officers and St. Lucie County Fire District personnel responded to the scene, along with fire engines, rescue vehicles and traffic cones blocking part of the intersection.

cards.headline: King's Landing development in Fort Pierce nears completion with luxury villas, Marriott Hotel by 2029
cards.teaser: The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing with construction milestones on ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage,
cards.body:
The King's Landing development project in downtown Fort Pierce is advancing with construction milestones on ten luxury villas, condos, retail spaces, restaurants, a parking garage, and a hotel. Brooke Harris, Team Lead of the Beachfront Brooke Team powered by Keller Williams Realty, said two residences have been sold and are nearing completion. Construction crews are almost finished with Villas 9 and 10, and the foundation has already been laid for Villas 7 and 8. The project includes a signed agreement with Marriott Hotel.

 The development is located in the waterfront district near the city marina and historic downtown Fort Pierce. Harris said the location provides walkability to shopping, restaurants, and retail, with boat storage available at the marina for residents. The project connects downtown to Edgartown.

 Michelle Chaffee Cavalcanti, executive director of Main Street Fort Pierce, said the development has the potential to impact local businesses by bringing in visitors and providing a place for families to stay. She said the project creates a destination where people can walk, shop, live, and play. Business owners are optimistic about having more residents in the downtown area with most amenities within walking distance.

 Chaffee Cavalcanti said the walkability means residents can visit a restaurant and then walk to another business afterwards to shop and get information. She said it becomes an experience and not just a singular destination. The estimated completion date is November 2029.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputy fired for Facebook post mocking sheriff's performance standards
cards.teaser: Deputy Tina Speicker was terminated after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance.
cards.body:
Deputy Tina Speicker was fired after an Internal Affairs investigation found she created a social media post that mocked Sheriff Richard Del Toro's Standards of Performance. According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Internal Affairs report, on Oct. 10, 2025, Sheriff Richard Del Toro was made aware of a Facebook post on Speicker's personal social media account featuring an image titled Standards of Power. The image closely resembled Del Toro's Standards of Performance, which was introduced after he was sworn into office.

 The report says Speicker's Facebook post mirrored the Standards of Performance but replaced the original language with phrases depicting domination, manipulation and exploitation. Investigators alleged the post was intended to disparage the Sheriff's Office and Sheriff Del Toro and violated agency rules and regulations. During the investigation, Speicker acknowledged posting the graphic to her Facebook page but said it was intended as commentary on Congress and the federal government shutdown.

 The report also found Speicker gave inconsistent statements during multiple interviews, leading investigators to sustain allegations of criticism of orders or policies, conduct unbecoming, violating the code of ethics for public officers and employees, and false testimony. As a result of the investigation, Speicker was terminated on June 12, 2026.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie apartment residents report unanswered maintenance requests, mold at Sanctuary at Winterlakes
cards.teaser: Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored.
cards.body:
Residents at Sanctuary at Winterlakes Apartments in Port St. Lucie said they have been living with unresolved maintenance issues and that their requests for help are being ignored. Alison Malio walked through her apartment pointing out what she believes is structural damage in her bedroom and damage she described as rot near the foundation. She also said her freezer seal was damaged and has cost her over $1,500 in lost food over the last year and a half to two years. Malio also showed a cockroach problem inside her apartment and building and said pest control only comes once every 13 weeks.

 Malio said she and her neighbors submit maintenance requests through an online portal, but she claims those requests go unanswered or get deleted and are sometimes marked complete even when no work has been done. Malio said she has cameras and a ring doorbell so she knows if maintenance comes to look at issues. She said it has been six or seven years of the property management doing nothing to help residents.

 Across the parking lot, neighbor Cheryl Jones said her air conditioning was out for nine weeks. Jones said it was too hot in her apartment to cook and she could only make breakfast with her coffee maker and toaster. Jones said maintenance eventually fixed the air conditioning, but mold had grown inside her apartment.

 Jones sent a report from a company that tested her unit and found evidence of mold, recommending that drywall, insulation and other materials be removed. Jones said she sent that report to property management but has not heard anything back.

 Property management sent a statement saying they are looking into the issues and that they prioritize the safety and well-being of tenants. When asked why they do not move, both Malio and Jones said they cannot afford to go anywhere else. Jones said she has nowhere to go.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce resort says abandoned sailboat is damaging property and costing thousands in revenue
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce resort says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago is damaging property and costing them thousands in business, but state law prevents them from moving it.
cards.body:
Dockside Marina and Resort in Fort Pierce says an abandoned sailboat that washed ashore three weeks ago near On The Edge Bar and Grill is damaging property, slamming into other boats, and costing them thousands in business. Joe Zebrowski, general manager of Dockside Marina and Resort, said the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission informed him that the boat cannot be moved. The agency is giving the owners 60 days to claim the vessel, and the resort is also prohibited from moving it.

 Zebrowski and his team quickly secured the boat when it washed ashore. The FWC used a chain to secure the sailboat, but Zebrowski said it has not stopped the vessel from causing problems. Zebrowski said the sailboat has slammed into a docked boat, destroyed a piling, and forced the restaurant to block off several tables near the vessel, which has significantly impacted their revenue. Zebrowski said the blocked tables are the restaurant's prime tables and have probably cost them about 25 percent of their overall business for the past month.

 According to state law, moving a boat that has washed ashore onto private property without proper permission can expose individuals to legal liabilities or even charges of theft. The FWC confirmed that no one can touch the boat except its owners.

cards.headline: Los Angeles man sentenced to life in prison for selling fentanyl that killed Vero Beach man
cards.teaser: Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of David Eller of Vero Beach. Guerrero was convicted by a fe
cards.body:
Alfonso Guerrero, 39, of Los Angeles was sentenced to life in federal prison for selling fentanyl that caused the death of David Eller of Vero Beach. Guerrero was convicted by a federal jury in May 2026 of distributing fentanyl resulting in death.

 Court evidence showed Guerrero sold a tenth of a gram of fentanyl to Eller on May 16, 2023, in a transaction captured on a doorbell camera. Eller was found dead in his Vero Beach home hours later. Two days after Eller's death, Guerrero was arrested with additional fentanyl intended for distribution.

 Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said the case demonstrates the commitment to holding drug dealers accountable. Flowers said the department will not tolerate drugs being sold in the community and praised detectives and federal partners for their investigative work.

 The case was investigated by the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and the DEA Miami Field Division. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida prosecuted the case.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers sworn in as chairman of Florida Sheriffs Association
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. F
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. Flowers now leads the statewide organization that brings together sheriffs from across Florida to develop strategies for leading their counties.

 The Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors includes sheriffs from throughout the state who work together on law enforcement strategies and leadership issues affecting county agencies. Flowers served as vice chairman of the board during the previous year before taking on the chairmanship role.

 The swearing-in ceremony took place Thursday, marking Flowers' elevation to the top position in the statewide law enforcement organization. The association serves as a platform for sheriffs to collaborate on policies and approaches to county law enforcement challenges.

 Flowers continues to serve as sheriff of Indian River County while taking on the additional responsibilities of chairing the Florida Sheriffs Association board. The organization coordinates efforts among the state's 67 elected sheriffs on issues ranging from training standards to legislative priorities.

cards.headline: Inmate awaiting retrial for Fort Pierce murder charged with attacking convicted killer in St. Lucie County Jail
cards.teaser: Robert Castro, 30, attacked convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside a St. Lucie County Jail dorm on July 6, knocking off his glasses and cutting his nose, according to an arrest affid
cards.body:
Robert Castro, 30, attacked convicted murderer Otto Lenke inside a St. Lucie County Jail dorm on July 6, knocking off his glasses and cutting his nose, according to an arrest affidavit filed July 20. Castro is awaiting a possible retrial in the fatal shooting of his former girlfriend, Taylor Ann Sato, outside her Timber Ridge Lane home in Fort Pierce in 2022.

 A jail sergeant witnessed Castro strike Lenke in the face, and surveillance video captured the attack. Lenke told a detective he had been using a jail-issued tablet to watch a chess game when Castro approached and hit him. A deputy noticed a cut on the upper part of Lenke's nose, and a nurse treated the injury.

 Castro refused to speak with investigators on July 16, repeatedly stating he did not understand his Miranda rights. He is now charged with battery by a person detained in a prison or jail facility, a felony.

 Lenke, a former Melbourne police officer and Indian River County firefighter, was convicted in May of first-degree murder and first-degree arson in the 2021 death of Richard Benson. Prosecutors said Lenke shot Benson three times inside Benson's Fort Pierce motorcycle shop, poured an accelerant on him and set him on fire while he was still alive. A jury voted 11-1 to recommend that Lenke be sentenced to death.

 Castro was convicted in 2024 of first-degree murder with a firearm in the death of Sato and sentenced to life in prison. The Fourth District Court of Appeal reversed his conviction in February after finding the trial court failed to properly complete the process for determining whether Castro was competent to stand trial. The appellate court ruled that a two-year-old evaluation was not sufficient because competency must be assessed close to the time of trial.

 The case was sent back to the trial court to determine whether Castro's competency during the 2024 trial can now be reliably evaluated. Castro would receive a new trial if a retrospective evaluation cannot be conducted or if the court determines he was not competent during the original trial.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art features American artists, new building exhibit through 2027
cards.teaser: More than 80 works by artists including Benjamin West, John Singer Sargent and Mary Cassatt are on display at Vero Beach Museum of Art through Aug. 16.
cards.body:
An exhibition titled American Made at Vero Beach Museum of Art includes more than 80 works by artists including Benjamin West, Sarah Miriam Peale, Edward Moran, John Singer Sargent, Mary Cassatt, Robert Henri and Charles Alston. The exhibit runs through Aug. 16 at the Holmes and Titelman Galleries at 3001 Riverside Park Drive in Vero Beach.

 Another exhibit, James Prosek: At Work, is on display at the museum's Holmes Gallery through Oct. 25. The exhibit features projects which define the artist's first 30 years of artmaking. Admission is free to members, children 17 and younger, and military veterans and active duty military with valid ID. Admission is $12 for adults, $11 for seniors and $5 for students with ID.

 The museum is also displaying Envisioning the New VBMA, an exhibit tracing the evolution of designs for the museum's new building and transformed campus created by Allied Works architecture and Unknown Studio Landscape Architecture Urban Design. That exhibit runs through Jan. 3, 2027.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Museum of Art to host recycled fishing line bracelet workshop Aug. 8
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will team up for a free Second Saturday program starting at 10 a.m. Aug. 8.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Museum of Art and Coastal Connections will host a free Second Saturday program beginning at 10 a.m. Aug. 8, with hands-on activities, gallery tours and lessons about protecting local marine life. Coastal Connections will lead a hands-on activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium, where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways.

 Participants also can learn about the Fishing Line Recycling Program. The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program.

 Visitors can then participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions. Guests also can tour the museum's summer exhibitions throughout the day. James Prosek: At Work is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day.
